# What the chatbot is

`r_chatbot` is a small conversational assistant written **entirely in R**. You type messages in a console, or in a Shiny chat window, and the bot — "Ada" — answers with full memory of the conversation.

The interesting part is what happens under the hood: the bot is not an R implementation of an AI agent. It delegates the AI work to the **langgraphr** package, which runs a graph engine in a hidden local background server. Your R code and your conversation never leave your machine — the only thing that travels to the AI provider is the message text sent by the hidden server when it needs a model reply.

The chatbot can:

- Chat with an OpenAI-compatible model (configured in `.env`)
- Remember the whole conversation (in-process, or durably in SQLite)
- Call **one R tool** (`session_info_tool`) when the user asks about their R environment
- Compress its own history every 10 messages so the context stays short

It cannot (by design): touch your data, files, or databases. It is chat + memory + one info tool.

# How it connects to langgraphr

The chatbot uses langgraphr's **assistant path**: a ready-made conversational agent created with `lg_connect()`.

```r
agent <- lg_connect()            # starts (or reuses) the hidden server
agent$add_tool(session_info_tool,
               description = "Report the user's R environment...")
res <- agent$invoke("Hello!")    # one full conversational turn
```

`lg_connect()` does two things. First, it makes sure the hidden server is running — if not, it starts it automatically as a supervised background process. Second, it returns an `LgAgent` object bound to a `thread_id`, which is the memory key for the conversation.

From that moment, the chatbot never manages any infrastructure. It only talks to langgraphr through three calls: `add_tool()`, `invoke()`, and `reset()`.

## The round trip of one message

When you type *"Hello"* and press Enter, this is the complete journey:

```
R session                 hidden local server           graph engine
-----------               -------------------           ------------
agent$invoke("Hello")
      |
      |-- POST /threads/<id>/runs -->  runs the assistant graph
      |                                on this thread's state
      |                                (the full message history)
      |
      |                          model wants an R tool?
      |                          the run PAUSES (interrupt)
      |  <-- interrupted -----------+
      |
  your R function runs locally
  (e.g. session_info_tool)
      |
      |-- POST /threads/<id>/resume ->  run continues with the
      |                                 tool's result
      |
      |  <-- completed -------------  final reply + updated state
reply shown to the user
```

Two properties of this design matter:

1. **R always starts the HTTP call.** The hidden server never calls back into R on its own, so there is no deadlock and no listener to set up.
2. **R tools run in your session.** When the model asks for a tool, the run pauses over HTTP, the R function executes locally with your environment, and the result is sent back. The engine only decides *when* to call a tool — the tool itself is ordinary R code.

# How a turn is produced

The Shiny front end runs each turn in a background R process so the interface never freezes while the model is thinking. The whole turn is one self-contained function in `R/graph.R`:

```r
chat_turn <- function(msg, thread_id, turn_count, personality,
                      seed = NULL, tools = list(), summary_every = 10L,
                      env_path = NULL, durable = FALSE, db_path = NULL) {
  library(langgraphr)
  # load credentials, enable SQLite memory when asked
  if (!is.null(env_path) && file.exists(env_path)) {
    try(dotenv::load_dot_env(env_path), silent = TRUE)
  }
  if (isTRUE(durable)) {
    if (is.null(db_path)) db_path <- "chatbot_memory.sqlite"
    lg_use_sqlite(db_path)
  }
  # reconnect to the SAME thread: the server restores this conversation
  agent <- lg_connect(thread_id = thread_id)
  for (t in tools) agent$add_tool(t$fn, description = t$description)
  # fresh thread: seed the personality first
  if (!is.null(seed) && nzchar(seed)) invisible(agent$invoke(seed))
  # the user's actual message
  res <- agent$invoke(msg)
  # summarize step (see below)
  ...
  list(content = res$content, note = note, thread_id = agent$thread_id)
}
```

The personality is not a special API feature — it is seeded as the **first message** of every fresh thread ("System note: you are Ada…"), so the instruction lives in the remembered history like every other message.

# How memory works

Memory is keyed by `thread_id`. Sending every message with the same id continues the same conversation, because the hidden server keeps each thread's full state — the message history — for as long as the server runs.

Two extras sit on top of that:

**Durable memory.** Calling `lg_use_sqlite("chatbot_memory.sqlite")` before the server starts points the engine at a SQLite file. Every thread's state is then written to disk, so conversations survive server restarts and R restarts. The Shiny app also saves the current thread id to `chatbot_thread_id.txt`, so re-opening the app resumes the same conversation; "New conversation" writes a fresh id and clears the view.

**The summarize step.** After every 10 user messages, the bot compresses its own history: it asks the model to summarize the current thread, switches to a new thread with `reset()`, and carries the summary in as the first message. Key facts survive; the context stays short.

# The two front ends

The brain lives in `R/graph.R`, `R/tools.R` and `R/utils.R`; two thin front ends share it.

| Front end | File | How it talks to langgraphr |
|---|---|---|
| Console | `main.R` | a `readline()` loop; `agent$invoke()` runs in the same process; `quit`/`exit` leave, `clear` resets memory |
| Shiny window | `app.R` | `shinychat` bubbles; each `invoke()` runs in a background R process via `callr` + promises, so the UI stays responsive while the model thinks |

The Shiny background design matters: a model reply takes seconds, and a blocking call would freeze the whole Shiny session long enough for the browser to show a "connection lost" overlay. Running the turn in a worker process keeps the interface live.

# Running it

One-time setup:

```r
remotes::install_local("LanggraphR")   # install the package from source
install.packages(c("dotenv", "R6", "cli", "shinychat"))
```

Put your credentials in `projects/r_chatbot/.env`:

```
LANGGRAPHR_MODEL=deepseek-v4-flash
LANGGRAPHR_API_KEY=sk-...
LANGGRAPHR_BASE_URL=https://api.deepseek.com
```

Then, in an R session:

```r
# console chat
source("projects/r_chatbot/main.R")

# or the chat window
shiny::runApp("projects/r_chatbot/app.R")
```

The first connection takes a few extra seconds (the hidden server starts and the personality is seeded). After that, each reply is a normal model round-trip.
